1:
The prophet lays his verdict down before he asks his question: God is righteous, and nothing following is a charge against him. Gill takes this as a first principle set deliberately in front, a truth he will not be moved from however unaccountable the providence looks; he notes that one old rendering turns the clause into a question — shall I dare to plead with thee at all? — while the Targum reverses it. Henry reads the clause as armour: the prophet arms himself before he parleys, because when God's dealings are darkest we fall back on general truths and hold them — he never did and never will wrong any creature.

Whether he was himself shaken is the first real disagreement. Gill grants he stood under the temptation that made the psalmist nearly slip, only more on his guard. Henry has him genuinely stumbling. Clarke says he was grieved that vice should be in affluence and piety in poverty, and wished to reason with God to be taught. Ellicott sets him beside the sufferers whose souls were vexed by the same anomaly in the divine government. Wesley splits the difference: not by way of accusing, but for his own satisfaction — the ways are just, but dark. Calvin dissents. He allows that this is how interpreters take it, but thinks something higher is in view: the prophets, seeing their labour spent on the intractable, turned their address to God as men who had given up on their hearers. The complaint is then indignation rather than confession, spoken past the deaf so they overhear that he has finished with them.

Who prospers is disputed only in scope. Henry and Keil and Delitzsch narrow it to hypocrites, men who have God on their lips and nowhere else; Ellicott ties the treacherous dealing to the conspirators of the preceding chapter; Clarke leaves it at vice in affluence. On the planting the split is sharper. Gill says all the good things even of the wicked come from God, who fixed the bounds of their settlement; Calvin agrees the prosperity is real and owed to blessing, though the figure here is not the planting of the elect. Ellicott alone treats the words as distrust speaking: they flourish so that one would think God had indeed planted them.

The third verse turns from them to himself. Keil and Delitzsch make the appeal precise: the phrase attaches to the heart and marks that heart's relation to God, so the plea is not that he is blameless but that God knows his fidelity, and the enmity he did nothing to earn. Gill lists what God knows — the sincerity, the office discharged, and that what his enemies say is calumny. Calvin insists he defends his commission and not his feelings, so the people contend with God and not a man. Ellicott hears the request as natural impatience, notes that prepare is better rendered devote and carries the idea of consecration, and observes that Jeremiah turns back on his enemies the figure of sheep for the slaughter they had used against him.

The last verse widens to the land. A drought lies behind the mourning ground and withered herb, and Keil and Delitzsch stress that the chastisement falls on innocent and guilty alike, on cattle and birds that earned none of it. Calvin turns that into an argument: if God has long punished beasts that have no fault, those whose fault it is cannot be spared. Clarke reads it as a prayer for removal — pull the sinners out and the land is delivered of what makes it desolate. The closing boast is a crux. Ellicott gives it as the taunt that they will outlive the prophet and never see him proved right, and records a variant behind the older Greek in which the boast is rather that God does not see their ways.
5:
The answer, when it comes, is two proverbs and a warning about family. Keil and Delitzsch treat both halves of the fifth verse as proverbial, contrasting a smaller task with a greater: if a race with footmen already tires him he cannot compete with horses, and what he suffered from his townsmen is a trifle against the assaults still awaiting him in his office. Clarke puts it more bluntly — if the smallest evils make him complain so bitterly, what will he feel under greater ones from enemies far more powerful. Ellicott has the prophet answering himself, the voice of the LORD heard in his inmost soul rebuking his impatience. Wesley reads it as preparation rather than reproof: greater dangers are coming, and the question is whether he can grapple with them.

Calvin refuses the rebuke outright. He reports that many take the words as God checking his prophet's boldness — thou hast contended with mortals and found the contest unequal, and darest now to assail me, who am greater than the world; the footmen have wearied thee, and thou art matched now against horsemen, that is, against me — and he rejects it. Jeremiah spoke not presumptuously nor from blind zeal but from a divine fervour, moved by God to rouse an obstinate people. Nothing in him needed checking.

What the two races stand for is disputed. Wesley makes the land of peace Anathoth, the land of his friends where he had a confidence, and the swelling of Jordan the capital, where the trouble will be worse; Calvin reports the same reading, the townsmen the footmen and the king, court, priests and people of the capital the horsemen, so that what he has met is only the beginning. Clarke ventures further, guessing the footmen for the Philistines and Edomites whose armies were mainly infantry and the horses for the Chaldeans with their cavalry — while granting in the same breath that the words are proverbial.

The swelling of Jordan itself is unsettled. Wesley and Clarke both know the annual overflow at harvest, but Clarke presses further: the flood drove the lions and other beasts from their coverts along the banks, and they spread through the country slaying men and carrying off cattle. Ellicott lays out both possibilities — the turbid stream over its banks, or the pride of Jordan meaning the jungle and its beasts, as the phrase seems to mean elsewhere — and declines to choose: commentators differ and there are no data for deciding. He adds that the English Version's supplied words are unnecessary, and would render the clause simply: in a land of peace thou art secure; what wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?

The sixth verse names the treachery. Gill takes the brethren for the men of Anathoth; Ellicott is not certain whether actual sons of one father are meant or only the men of that town as a section of the priesthood, and thinks earlier language in the book favours the literal sense. Calvin reads it as amplification — not the citizens of the capital only, but his own relations, who dealt with a brother no more courteously than strangers would. Wesley has both his town and his family conspiring secretly. On the shouting all agree it is a hue and cry: Ellicott would render it a full shout raised after him, and Calvin observes that to cry after a man who has turned his back and declined the fight marks a settled hatred rather than ordinary enmity. Clarke draws the conclusion — he has none to depend on but God, and must not commit himself to them, for they are enemies at heart whatever fair words they use. Ellicott adds that the saying about a prophet having no honour in his own country and his own house probably had its origin here.
7:
God answers the complaint with a heavier one. Ellicott supplies the connecting thought where he can find one — what are thy sufferings beside those I have brought on mine heritage? — while confessing the join is unclear, and suggesting the chapter may be fragments written at intervals and later arranged without headings. Keil and Delitzsch record the same unease in others, who denied any connection with what precedes and would cut the closing oracle loose as a piece from a later reign; they judge that a wrong conception of the passage.

The house forsaken is the temple, and the voices differ only on how far the word reaches. Henry has God driven from his own palace by their pollution of it: they were the beloved of his soul and returned him hatred for his love. Clarke makes it a covenant term — forsaking him meant abandonment to their enemies and expulsion from the good land. Wesley reads the heritage as the whole people, left as to God's special providence. Gill takes the temple in two fulfilments: the first when the Chaldeans destroyed it, and more fully the second, when Christ took his leave and a voice was heard within before the city fell. Calvin alone widens the word: the whole country was reckoned God's habitation on the temple's account, safe under its shadow, so the forsaking reaches land and people entire. He hears a string of concessions — ye are his house, his heritage, his beloved, his richest portion, and none of it keeps him from judging you.

The metaphors then turn on the heritage itself. As a lion it roars against its owner: Gill hears the clamour against providence and the rage against the prophets, Clarke the flagrancy of the acts, Calvin a wild beast attacking God himself, so that he stands in his own patrimony as in a vast forest. Ellicott alone handles the hard clause carefully — the mood was unlovable, and so, after the manner of men, the love turned to hatred.

The speckled bird divides them four ways. Gill offers the old reading of a many-coloured bird, beautiful as a peacock, but presses the word toward dipped or stained: a bird of prey marked with others' blood, an emblem of a people who shed the blood of prophets. Clarke reads the colours as the borrowed rites of the nations, so each nation whose gods they took up comes to reclaim its own, and cites the fable of the daw in borrowed plumes. Ellicott insists the Hebrew is a question and that both words mean birds of prey, the speckled one some uncommon vulture, and grounds the image in observed bird life — birds of one kind mobbing a solitary stranger of another, jackals coming up behind. Wesley states the habit plainly: birds flock about a strange-coloured bird they have not seen before. Calvin dismisses the variegated and blood-stained readings alike as having no appearance of correctness, and takes speckled to mean wild — a bird of the wood, against tame creatures that keep to their cages and folds, which is what he meant this people to be.

The pastors who destroyed the vineyard are foreign; their range is the question. Gill says they are not the people's own governors, civil or religious, but heathen princes, naming the Chaldean king and his generals. Clarke spreads them across the whole history of the invasions. Ellicott objects to the word, since the modern associations of pastors sit badly on men reckless and destructive, and draws instead nomad herdsmen breaking the fence and turning flocks in on the tender shoots — shepherds rather than a wild boar, because shepherds carry the thought of a systematic plan. Calvin finds an antithesis: God had been their shepherd and would have stayed so; because they could not bear him, other shepherds will come who treat them as they please.
11:
Three times in one breath the land is called desolate, and Ellicott hears the repetition as a sound before a statement: the Hebrew word, so uttered, must have come out as a wail of lamentation. Who did the desolating is less settled than the fact. Ellicott takes the verb as impersonal — one has made it desolate, that is, it is made desolate. Wesley refuses that: the Hebrew reads he hath made it, and it cannot be God, who is the speaker and named in the next words; so it is the Chaldean king as instrumental cause, or the people and their rulers as the meritorious one. Calvin, noticing the same change of number, presses it the other way — not merely the united army but every individual in it would be their master, free to vex and devour at pleasure; and he records the older versions that make the verb passive and singular. Gill takes the repetition for certainty.

The neglect is the sting. Clarke says the desolations are so plainly the consequence of the people's crimes that not laying them to heart is the wonder, the only cure being repentance. Ellicott sharpens the tense — no man laid it to heart — so the past neglect bears fruit in the present misery. Wesley makes that failure a great cause of the judgment itself, and Calvin hears in the phrase a touch at the torpor of his own nation.

What the spoilers climb is disputed. Ellicott takes the high places for the bare treeless heights so often chosen for an idolatrous sanctuary. Gill takes them for fortified places that could not withstand the invaders, and notes a rendering giving instead the plains in the wilderness, pasture trodden down and made forage. Calvin insists the word is not uninhabited solitude but upland fit for pasture, set against the level country: once the enemy had rambled the plains, no recess however hidden would be safe. He reads the closing clause the same way, against men who hoped a limited victory would satisfy the invader — the wrath would burn through rich and poor, countryman and citizen alike. Ellicott narrows it, holding the context to limit the sentence to the offenders of the cities of Judah, and noting that flesh here carries its sense of human nature as corrupt.

On the sword itself Ellicott and Clarke agree and put it differently. Ellicott sets the phrase beside the old battle cry in which a man's work in war is instrumental to a will mightier than his own: the invader's sword was, after all, God's sword. Clarke draws the practical edge — it is the sword of the LORD that has devoured and will devour, and this is what no man lays to heart, because they think such things come in the course of events.

The wheat and the thorns are the chapter's last figure, and the readings are old. Gill runs through them: a literal curse on the ground; the prophets sowing good seed and finding evil works spring up; prayers unaccepted for want of repentance. He prefers the people's own schemes, the alliance sought with Egypt against the Chaldeans, which proved thorns; and he mentions a pointing that reads the verb as the imperative sow ye, taken ironically. Calvin calls the prophets reading strained and lands where Gill does — they sowed by seeking aid here and there and strengthening themselves with confederacies, and thought themselves wise; the prophet grants the sowing only to laugh the confidence to scorn. Clarke and Wesley keep it general: every project fails, every counsel profits nothing. Ellicott corrects the tense, have reaped thorns and profited nothing, so the sentence of failure is already written; he notes that revenues meant produce and not money when the English was made, and that the shame is likelier the conquered people's disappointed increase than the conquerors' scanty spoil.
14:
A new message opens. The neighbours are the surrounding nations, and the rosters differ: Gill names the Egyptians, Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites and Edomites, and explains both words — neighbours because they lay close to the land where God's people dwelt, evil because they so often distressed it. Henry gives a shorter list but a longer charge: they were evil neighbours first in helping to debauch Israel, and now help make her desolate and join the Chaldeans against her. What is done against his church God takes as done against himself, and it is just with him to make those the instruments of our trouble whom we made instruments of our sin. Ellicott names those who rejoiced in Judah's fall and struck her in her weakness, and observes that the prophet, burning against his own people, is angrier at these outsiders.

Whether these verses belong where they stand is disputed. Clarke separates them outright as a different discourse, dated to the seventh or eighth year of Jehoiakim; Keil and Delitzsch report a related move in others, who take the preceding strophe for a lament over plundering already suffered, not a prophecy.

Clarke supplies the hardest illustration: God uses one wicked nation to scourge another and then scourges the scourger, and being made the executor of his justice is no proof of his approbation — as a condemned felon is made the county hangman while still under sentence, till a brother of the trade does for him what he did for others.

The plucking is then reversed, and the surprise is who benefits. Ellicott insists the compassion is not for Judah only but for the evil neighbours, and marks the asymmetry: they are plucked from their own land, Judah from the land of her exile. His appetite for retribution is overpowered by a new love that does not exclude even these, though their deliverance will be less signal than hers. Calvin makes the same extension and turns it to comfort: the faithful look not only for their own salvation but for their enemies', whom God will gather with them, so his favour is doubled rather than obscured. Wesley keeps both halves, the sword and captivity and then a fetching out; Gill times it after they have lain captive some while.

The condition is a change of religion, and swearing stands for all of it. Keil and Delitzsch explain why: an oath is among the chief utterances of a religious confession, so to swear in the name of the LORD is to adopt his worship, and those who do are built in and blessed with his people. Ellicott adds the moral qualification — the acknowledgment must be reverent and righteous, not hypocritical — and points out the reversal: these nations had taught God's people to swear by Baal, and are now to be led by her example. Wesley states it plainly: leave idolatry and pay homage to the living and true God. Calvin reads the ways of the people as what God commanded rather than what they practised, since they often departed from it. Gill alone turns the phrase toward the church of his own day: the ways learned by attendance on word and ordinances, obedience a hearkening to gospel ministers.

On the last verse they converge. Refusal meets utter destruction, and Ellicott hears in the verb the prophet's own commission, the very word rendered root out when he was called. Keil and Delitzsch call the promise Messianic, pointing to the end of God's way with all nations; Clarke and Wesley find in it the conversion of the Gentiles, Clarke adding that several of these nations did not obey and are gone, no vestige of them remaining. Calvin sees the threat aimed past the nations at the Jews: if God could not bear the perverseness of Gentiles who did not know him, those who imbibed his law from infancy can hardly escape.
